blocks.text: Constitutional authorities are bodies **created directly by the Constitution** — their composition, appointment, removal and independence safeguards are constitutionally entrenched, unlike statutory bodies (created by Acts, e.g., NHRC, CVC, CBI) or executive bodies (e.g., NITI Aayog). They are the **fourth-branch guardians**: umpires of elections, public finance, recruitment and social justice.

rows: Superintendence, direction, control of elections to Parliament, legislatures, President/VP
CEC removable only like an SC judge; service conditions not variable to disadvantage; **CEC & ECs (Appointment) Act, 2023** — selection by PM, LoP, a Union Minister (after **Anoop Baranwal, 2023**)
Audits all Union/state accounts; 'guardian of the public purse' (Ambedkar: the most important officer)
6-yr/65-age tenure; removal like SC judge; salary charged on Consolidated Fund; ineligible for further government office
Merit recruitment, disciplinary advice, service matters
Fixed 6-yr terms; removal only by President after SC inquiry (even for SPSC members)
First law officer of Union / State; right of audience in all courts

Removal like a High Court judge

sections.heading: Roles in action — and stress points

items: **ECI**: Model Code of Conduct enforcement, symbol allotment, deciding disqualification references (Art 103 with President). Stress points: appointment process (partially fixed by the 2023 Act, criticised for executive majority in the panel), MCC's non-statutory character, electoral-roll disputes.

**CAG**: performance audits (2G, coal) reshaped accountability; reports go to President/Governor → laid before House → **Public Accounts Committee** examines. Stress: post-facto audit only, no power over PSU subsidiaries' choice, appointments opaque.

**PSCs**: consulted on recruitment and discipline (**Art 320** — advisory only, but departures must be reported to the House). Stress: expanding exempted posts, delays in exams — an acute AP theme (APPSC calendar reliability).

**Finance Commission**: the fiscal umpire — **15th FC (N.K. Singh): 41% devolution**, sectoral and local-body grants; the **16th FC (Arvind Panagariya)** reports for 2026–31. Stress: ToR controversies, cesses bypassing the divisible pool.
**NCSC/NCST/NCBC**: civil-court powers but recommendations non-binding; annual reports tabled late.

items: **APPSC** (Art 315) conducts Group-I/II services; its independence, calendar and paper-setting quality are perennial public issues — cite the Commission's constitutional protections when discussing reform.

**AP State Election Commission** made national headlines in 2020–21 when local-body election scheduling triggered a confrontation with the state government — the SC upheld SEC autonomy (following **Kishansing Tomar** logic).
**AP Advocate-General (Art 165)** and the **AP Finance Commission (SFC)** complete the state-level mirror of Union authorities.
The **Fifth Schedule + NCST** oversight matters for AP's agency areas (tribal sub-plan, land-transfer regulations 1 of 70).

blocks.text: Exam tip: When asked about 'constitutional authorities and their role', do not catalogue endlessly — pick ECI, CAG, PSCs, FC as the four pillars, one live controversy each (2023 CEC Act, PAC follow-up gap, exempted posts, cess bypass), then close with the distinction from statutory bodies. Precision on article numbers is what separates top answers.

blocks.text: **AP dimension:** the **AP Public Service Commission (Art 315)** is the recruiting spine of state governance; **Art 371D** created the **AP Administrative Tribunal** and the local-cadre/Presidential-Order regime. Cite the CAG's audits of state schemes and the State Finance Commission (Art 243-I) to localise accountability answers.

prelimsPointers: **CEC and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023** — selection panel: PM, a Union Cabinet Minister, and the Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha.
**CAG (Art 148)** — audits under the CAG's (DPC) Act, 1971; reports to the President/Governor, examined by the PAC/COPU.
**Art 324** vests superintendence of elections in ECI; multi-member since 1993; CEC + 2 ECs with equal powers, decisions by majority.
**Anoop Baranwal v. Union (2023)**: SC-devised panel (PM, LoP, CJI) until Parliament legislated; the **2023 Act** replaced CJI with a Union Minister.
**CAG** submits Union audit reports to the **President (Art 151)**; state reports to the Governor.
**Art 320** consultation with PSC is **advisory**; exceptions listed in Art 320(3) provisos and Regulations.
**NCBC** became constitutional via the **102nd Amendment (2018)**; the **105th Amendment (2021)** restored states' power to notify their own backward classes.
SPSC members are appointed by the **Governor** but removable only by the **President** (Art 317).
**16th Finance Commission** chair: **Arvind Panagariya**; award period 2026–31.
mainsAngles: 'Independent constitutional authorities are the fourth branch of government' — examine with reference to the ECI and CAG.
Has the CEC and ECs (Appointment) Act, 2023 secured or diluted the Election Commission's independence? Evaluate post-Anoop Baranwal.
The CAG's audit is a post-mortem without a follow-up surgery — discuss the accountability chain from audit report to PAC to action taken.
Assess the constitutional design of State Public Service Commissions and the reforms APPSC needs to command aspirant confidence.

glossary.definition: An authority created by the Constitution itself (e.g., ECI, CAG, UPSC, FC), as distinct from statutory bodies created by legislation (NHRC, CVC) or executive resolutions (NITI Aayog).
Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund (e.g., salaries of CAG, judges) — discussable but non-votable in the House, insulating the office from annual majority pressure.
ECI's consensual, non-statutory norms binding parties and governments from election announcement to results; enforced through Art 324's plenary power.
22-member parliamentary committee (15 LS + 7 RS), chaired by an Opposition member, that examines CAG reports — the audit's legislative teeth.
Removal procedure for PSC members: only by the President, on the Supreme Court's inquiry report finding misbehaviour — a key independence safeguard.

blocks.text: **Parliament (Art 79)** = **President + Rajya Sabha + Lok Sabha**. Lok Sabha: maximum **550** elected (530 states + 20 UTs; the Anglo-Indian nomination ended with the **104th Amendment, 2019**); term 5 years. Rajya Sabha: maximum **250** (238 elected by state assemblies via **proportional representation by single transferable vote** + 12 nominated); permanent House, **one-third retiring every two years**. State legislature (**Art 168**) = Governor + Assembly (+ Council where it exists). **Andhra Pradesh is bicameral**: Assembly of **175**, Council of **58** (Art 171 composition: 1/3 by MLAs, 1/3 by local bodies, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated).

rows: Presides over LS; decides money-bill certification (**Art 110(3)** — final), anti-defection references (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992** — judicially reviewable); casting vote only
Gap between sessions cannot exceed **6 months**; Budget, Monsoon, Winter by convention
For ordinary-bill deadlock; presided by Speaker; used thrice (Dowry 1961, Banking 1978, POTA 2002); NOT for money or constitution-amendment bills

sections.heading: Conduct of business — how the Houses actually work

items: **Question Hour** (starred/unstarred/short-notice) and **Zero Hour** (an Indian innovation, no rules basis) are the daily accountability instruments.
**Motions**: adjournment (censure device, LS only), no-confidence (Rule 198, 50 members), censure, calling-attention, **short-duration discussion (Rule 193)** — no vote.

**Legislative procedure**: bill → readings → committee (optional) → other House → assent (**Art 111**: President may return once; must assent on repassage). **Money bill (Art 110)**: only LS votes; RS returns within **14 days** with recommendations; Speaker's certificate. **Finance-Act-as-money-bill** misuse questioned in **Rojer Mathew (2019)** — referred to a larger bench.

**Budget process (Art 112)**: presentation → general discussion → **Departmentally Related Standing Committees' scrutiny (24 DRSCs since 1993)** → demands for grants, cut motions → Appropriation Act → Finance Act; **guillotine** closes undiscussed demands.

**Committees do the real work**: PAC, Estimates, Committee on Public Undertakings; DRSCs; but the share of bills referred to committees fell from ~71% (15th LS) to under 20% recently — a standard 'decline of Parliament' data point along with fewer sitting days (~55–60/year vs 120+ in the 1950s) and rising disruptions.

sections.heading: Functioning: decline and renewal — with the AP mirror

items: **Symptoms of decline**: shrinking sittings, ordinance raj (**Art 123/213**; SC in **Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017** — re-promulgation is a fraud on the Constitution), guillotined budgets, bypassed committees, disruptions replacing debate, and the **money-bill route** around the Rajya Sabha.

**State assemblies sit far less** — many, including AP's, average 20–30 days a year; Council utility debated (AP's Council was abolished in 1985 and revived in 2007; abolition was again resolved by the Assembly in 2020 under **Art 169** but lapsed without parliamentary action — a unique living example of Art 169 mechanics).

**Renewal agenda**: minimum sitting calendar (NCRWC suggested 120/60 days), mandatory committee reference, post-legislative scrutiny, Speaker's neutrality conventions, digital Sansad/e-Vidhan (**AP Assembly runs e-Vidhan under NeVA**).

blocks.text: Exam tip: Questions on 'structure and functioning' reward institutional data — sitting days, % bills to committees, three joint sittings, 104th Amendment — plus one AP hook: the 2020 Art 169 Council-abolition resolution that lapsed. Learn the money-bill vs finance-bill distinction cold; it is a favourite.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — a declining Parliament, by the numbers

items: **Fewer sitting days:** Lok Sabha now sits far below the ~120–130 days a year of the 1950s–60s; many bills are passed with limited debate and **declining reference to committees**.

**Disruptions & the 'ordinance route':** frequent adjournments and heavy use of **Art 123/213 ordinances** weaken deliberation; the **Money Bill route (Art 110)** — used for Aadhaar and amendments — bypasses the Rajya Sabha and is contested (*Rojer Mathew*, *Roger* referred to a larger bench).

**Anti-defection (Tenth Schedule):** consolidates party discipline but curbs the individual member's voice; *Kihoto Hollohan* (1992) made the Speaker's disqualification decision judicially reviewable and later verdicts urged deciding within a reasonable time.

**New Parliament & women's reservation:** the **106th Amendment (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam, 2023)** reserves one-third of Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats for women — effective after delimitation following the next census.

prelimsPointers: **106th Amendment (2023)** — one-third reservation for women in Lok Sabha & State Assemblies; contingent on delimitation post-census.
**Money Bill** defined in **Art 110**; Speaker certifies; Rajya Sabha can only recommend (14 days).
mainsAngles: 'Indian legislatures are deliberating less and disrupting more' — analyse the decline in legislative effectiveness and suggest reforms.

prelimsPointers: Rajya Sabha election: **proportional representation by single transferable vote**; open ballot since 2003; domicile requirement removed (2003), upheld in **Kuldip Nayar (2006)**.
**Art 85**: maximum 6-month gap between sessions — no fixed number of sessions is prescribed.
Joint sittings held only **three times**: Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission repeal (1978), POTA (2002).
**Money bill (Art 110)** can be introduced **only in Lok Sabha, on the President's recommendation**; Speaker's certification treated as final (contested in Rojer Mathew, 2019).
**104th Amendment (2019)** ended Anglo-Indian nominated seats; SC/ST reservation in LS/Assemblies extended (now to 2030 via the 126th Amendment Bill route → 104th CAA).
AP Legislative Council: **58 members**, created under **Art 169** (revived 2007); Assembly strength **175** (Reorganisation Act allows increase to 225, pending delimitation).
**Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**: repeated re-promulgation of ordinances is unconstitutional.
mainsAngles: 'Parliament is becoming a forum for announcement rather than deliberation' — critically evaluate with data on sittings, committees and ordinances.
Distinguish money bills from financial bills and examine the constitutional concerns over money-bill certification.
Do Legislative Councils add deliberative value or partisan delay? Assess with Andhra Pradesh's abolition-revival-abolition history under Article 169.
Evaluate the role of Departmentally Related Standing Committees in restoring legislative scrutiny, and suggest reforms.

glossary.definition: The period immediately after Question Hour when members raise urgent matters without prior notice — an Indian procedural innovation with no mention in the Rules.
The Speaker's putting of all outstanding demands for grants to vote at once when allotted budget time expires, foreclosing discussion.

Law promulgated by President/Governor when the legislature is not in session; must be laid before the House and lapses 6 weeks after reassembly; re-promulgation condemned in Krishna Kumar Singh (2017).
Device to reduce a demand for grant — policy cut (Re 1), economy cut (specified amount), token cut (₹100) — symbolising executive accountability in financial matters.

Parliament may create or abolish a state Legislative Council if the Assembly so resolves by special majority — the provision behind AP's Council's abolition (1985), revival (2007) and pending 2020 abolition resolution.

blocks.text: Parliamentary privileges are **special rights and immunities enjoyed by each House collectively and members individually**, so that legislatures can function 'without let or hindrance'. Source: **Arts 105 (Parliament) and 194 (state legislatures)**. Two privileges are **expressly written**: (1) **freedom of speech in the House** — no court proceedings for anything said or any vote given (Art 105(2)); (2) **right to publish proceedings** (protection extended to true press reports by the **Parliamentary Proceedings (Protection of Publication) Act, 1977** and **Art 361A**). All other privileges were to be defined by law — Parliament never has, so they remain those of the **House of Commons at the commencement of the Constitution** (via the 44th Amendment's frozen reference).

rows: Freedom of speech in the House; **freedom from arrest in civil cases** 40 days before/after and during session; exemption from jury/witness duty while in session

Right to publish/expunge proceedings; **exclude strangers**; secret sittings; **punish for contempt/breach of privilege** (including non-members); immediate information of a member's arrest; regulate internal proceedings (**Art 122/212** — courts cannot inquire into procedural irregularity)

sections.heading: The classic clashes — cases you must cite

items: **G.K. Reddy / Gunupati (1954)** & **Pandit M.S.M. Sharma v. Sri Krishna Sinha (Searchlight, 1959)**: privilege (expunged proceedings) prevailed over **Art 19(1)(a)**; but privileges are subject to **Art 21**.

**Keshav Singh's case (UP, 1964 — Presidential Reference)**: judges cannot be hauled up for privilege when they entertain a habeas petition; uneasy truce between courts and Houses — privileges are subject to **fundamental rights and judicial review at the jurisdictional threshold**.

**P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**: bribe-taking MPs who voted enjoyed immunity — **overruled by the seven-judge bench in Sita Soren v. Union (2024)**: **bribery is not protected** by Arts 105/194; the offence is complete on acceptance.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: expulsion for cash-for-query upheld; the House's power to punish is real but judicially reviewable for illegality/unconstitutionality.
**Amarinder Singh (2010)**: privilege cannot punish acts outside the House's functioning.
**State of Kerala v. K. Ajith (2021)**: privilege is **no immunity from criminal law** — MLAs who vandalised the House could not have prosecution withdrawn.

sections.heading: Issues arising — and the reform debate

items: **Uncodified privileges** breed uncertainty and chill the press — the NCRWC and press commissions have recommended **codification**; Houses resist, fearing judicial review of every claim.
**Privilege vs free speech of citizens**: notices against journalists and critics (several state assemblies, including undivided AP's episodes) raise proportionality concerns.
**Punitive contempt power without due process**: the House is complainant, prosecutor and judge; Raja Ram Pal offers only outer-limit review.

**Anti-defection interface**: the Speaker's privilege-cum-tribunal roles (Kihoto) concentrate power; **Keisham Meghachandra (2020)** urged a 4-week outer limit and an independent tribunal for defection cases.
**Balanced way forward**: codify core privileges, time-bound privilege committees, restrict contempt to actual obstruction of the House, and preserve absolute in-House speech — the deliberative core.

blocks.text: Exam tip: 'Powers, privileges and issues arising' = definition + two written privileges + three landmark cases (Searchlight, Keshav Singh, Sita Soren) + codification debate. The 2024 Sita Soren overruling of P.V. Narasimha Rao is the single most exam-worthy update — never omit it.

sections.heading: 🏛 Deep mastery — privileges vs free press & the codification debate

blocks.text: Parliamentary privileges (**Arts 105/194**) remain **uncodified** — drawn from those of the House of Commons at commencement. Key clashes to cite: **Keshav Singh (1965)** (UP Assembly vs judiciary on committal for contempt); **Raja Ram Pal (2007)** (cash-for-query expulsion upheld — House has power to expel); and the recent **Sita Soren (2024)** verdict where a 7-judge bench **overruled *P.V. Narasimha Rao* (1998)** to hold that legislators taking bribes are **NOT immune** under Art 105(2)/194(2) — a landmark for probity.

**The unresolved question — codification:** critics argue uncodified privileges create uncertainty and can chill press freedom; defenders say codification would invite constant judicial intrusion into House autonomy. A balanced answer favours a **narrowly codified, rights-compatible framework** consistent with Art 19(1)(a).

prelimsPointers: **Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)** — 7-judge bench held bribe-taking MPs/MLAs have NO immunity under Arts 105(2)/194(2); overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
Parliamentary privileges under **Arts 105 & 194** remain **uncodified**.

Privileges flow from **Arts 105 & 194**; the phrase 'freedom of speech in Parliament' is subject to constitutional provisions and House rules (e.g., **Art 121** — no discussion of judges' conduct except on a removal motion).
Freedom from arrest covers **civil cases only** — 40 days before and after a session; no immunity in criminal or preventive-detention matters.
**Art 361A** protects true reports of parliamentary/legislative proceedings.
**Sita Soren (2024, 7 judges)** overruled **P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**: no privilege immunity for bribery for a speech or vote.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: expulsion upheld; House punishment judicially reviewable on limited grounds.
Courts cannot question House proceedings for **procedural irregularity (Arts 122/212)** — but can for illegality or unconstitutionality.
The **Privileges Committee**: 15 members in LS (10 in RS), appointed by the presiding officer.
mainsAngles: 'Uncodified privileges sit uneasily with a codified Constitution' — critically examine the case for codifying legislative privileges.
Trace the judicial journey from Searchlight to Sita Soren on the reach of legislative privileges.
Privilege is meant to protect the House's functioning, not members from the criminal law — discuss with recent case law.
Examine the tension between the citizen's Article 19(1)(a) rights and the House's contempt power, with suggestions for balance.

glossary.definition: Violation of any individual or collective right of the House or its members (e.g., misreporting proceedings, obstructing members), punishable by the House through admonition, reprimand or imprisonment.
Any act or omission that obstructs the House's work or lowers its dignity — broader than breach of privilege; may be committed even where no specific privilege is violated.

glossary.term: Freedom of speech in the House
glossary.definition: Absolute immunity of members from court proceedings for anything said or any vote given in the House (Arts 105(2)/194(2)) — the deliberative core of legislative privilege.
Bar on courts inquiring into legislative proceedings on the ground of procedural irregularity; substantive illegality remains reviewable (Raja Ram Pal).

glossary.term: Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024)
glossary.definition: Seven-judge decision holding that bribery in connection with a speech or vote is not protected by Articles 105/194, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
